one_pager.big_idea: One result can fool us, so we repeat, calculate the mean and range, and ask whether a difference is bigger than the normal variation.
goals: I can carry out a fair ruler-drop test with five repeats per hand and calculate the mean and range.
I can write a conclusion that says whether a difference is big enough to matter, mentioning uncertainty.

flow.what: Two retrieval questions answered on the back of the worksheet: which bias in 'I only remember the days my lucky pen worked' (confirmation bias) and the mean of 12, 15, 11, 14 cm (13 cm). Slides 1 to 2.

Teacher drops the 15 cm PRIZE strip between a volunteer's finger and thumb (held at the middle); repeat with 2 or 3 volunteers; most miss. Then the claim 'Your dominant hand reacts faster than your other hand': vote Yes, No or No difference. Slides 3 to 4.

Name the variables (change which hand; measure catch distance, then reaction time; keep the same ruler, dropper, starting position, no warning); demonstrate the ruler drop with a student using the picture steps; show the conversion table and how to calculate mean and range (0.17, 0.16, 0.17, 0.15, 0.16 s: mean 0.16 s, range 0.02 s). Slides 5 to 8.

Safety slide read aloud in both languages. In pairs: 5 drops per hand per person, alternating hands, record cm and convert to seconds (partner 1 for 6 min, partner 2 for 6 min); then calculate mean and range (6 min); Stretch and Challenge. Teacher checks the 0 cm mark is level with the top of the thumb, the wait is random and hands alternate. Slides 9 to 10. If short: 3 repeats per hand, skip the Challenge formula check.

Overlap diagram: 'Is the difference big enough?' Students decide whether their own difference is bigger than their range and share with a frame; class count (dominant faster, other faster, same): 'Is that enough to give a verdict?'; exit ticket and logbook line. Slides 11 to 12. If short: class count with hands up.

one_pager.practical: Ruler-drop reaction test in pairs: the dropper holds a 30 cm ruler with the 0 cm mark level with the top of the seated catcher's thumb, waits 1 to 5 seconds and lets go without warning; the catcher reads the cm at the top of the thumb. Five drops per hand, alternating hands; each distance is converted to a time with the table, then mean and range are calculated for each hand.
one_pager.assessment: Results table with mean and range, and a conclusion that mentions uncertainty (Stretch). Spot-check 6 worksheets for correct range calculation (range errors feed into Week 5 checkpoint question 6). Exit ticket: mean (0.18 s), range (0.05 s) and one verdict (best answer: Not supported). Logbook line: 'My dominant hand was ___ by ___ s, which is / is not bigger than my range.'
hazards: Low hazard. Rulers can hit faces or fingers if flicked or swung: hold the ruler upright and still; never flick, swing or throw it.
Falling ruler near the face: keep your face away from the ruler when it drops.
Leaning or standing can lead to bumps and falls: sit down for every test.
one_pager.language_note: Frames: 'My dominant hand mean was ___ s and my other hand mean was ___ s.' 'The data suggests ___; however, ___.' 'To be more confident, we would need ___.' 'Our verdict is ___ because ___.' Chinese talk is welcome in pairs during the test; readings are called out in English numbers ('fourteen centimetres'). Traps: 'range' in everyday English means a choice of things, in maths it is one number (biggest minus smallest), 极差 not 范围; 'mean' is not 'means' (method); catching a ruler is a reaction, not a reflex (a reflex is automatic).
watch_out: Range errors are the most common: students write '0.15 to 0.17' instead of subtracting. Insist on one number.
Droppers who drop in a rhythm: catchers learn it and 'catch' impossibly fast (under 5 cm). Repeat those tries; the wait must be random, 1 to 5 seconds.
'A bigger distance means faster' and 'any difference in the means proves the claim': the ruler falls further when you are slower, and small differences can be normal variation.
If the ruler falls past 30 cm, write 'missed' and do that try again; a try with a slip or a warning does not count.
one_pager.next_week_link: Next week (Week 4, Correlation or cause) moves from comparing two groups to looking for patterns between two variables. The PRIZE winner has first choice of role next week.
